comments.author: @Anna-mv9ew
comments.text: Very interesting news! For using open-source models you still need to provide a lot of context, and context window is a big culprit. So you have to use RAGs, but they lose important context and information as well, can lose something very important. Fine-tuning comes to mind, but there's literally no success stories on this front, you cannot fine-tune the whole model even as an enterprise unless you're OpenAI/grok/etc (unimaginable compute needed), and if you fine-tune just a fraction of weights (like it's typically done) the model doesn't actually learn, it just alters its style, which might reflect in some surface-level highly imperfect learning. So, to conclude, it is not straightforward to use open-source, or probably any, ai for complex projects

comments.author: @ChrisBensler
comments.text:
I've been programming since the early 90's and have been interested in and loosely following AI advancements since then.
None of this LLM tech is very surprising and if you know how it works, you understand why it's way more hype than fact.

This AI advent is even MORE reason to get into SWE, not less, if you're actually any good at it.
If you thought that an SWE job would be a free ride career, then maybe you should be sad. Hopefully AI will put a lot of pressure on the lower end of the SWE career market and restore the tough barrier to entry. There's far too many useless tits who can copy-pasta. These are the people AI can replace. AI is great at copy-pasta.

All of the tech we are seeing today is not really new, except that we now have the compute power to do useful things.
Most of  these 'breakthroughs' are just people trying to capitalize. They'd sell you the moon and assure you it can fit in your pocket, if they could get away with it.

AI may be able to replace some coding, but it's not enough just to produce code that manages to work.
Human SWE will be even more important. Script kiddies may be out of a job, if their role is merely to churn code.
None of these AI do very good in the real world, outside of these staged tests in very controlled environments with very controlled tasks and results. The real world doesn't work this way. Half the job of negotiating a software project is figuring out what the client actually wants and needs, not just iterating until you stumble in the right direction.

comments.author: @coleshores
comments.text:
I believe AI will be a powerful tool for those with strong engineering skills. For instance, an engineer could design an architecture using Terraform to integrate Athena, Glue, and S3 for parsing S3 flow logs, then develop a Python script to execute Athena queries for analysis. While AI can generate each of these components individually, it lacks the creativity to seamlessly integrate them into a cohesive solution.

As a result, senior engineers will likely shift toward more managerial roles, delegating these tasks to AI for implementation. However, AI also has the potential to make novice engineers appear more capable than they actually are, which could lead to downward wage pressure in the industry over the coming years.
